summary: Describes the MINIMAL addressing method, which encodes telephone-network (PSTN) numbers into ordinary email addresses, plus a standard way to add further elements later. It supports services that reach phones through email gateways. It was replaced by RFC 3191.

eli5.summary: A way to write a phone number so it looks like an email address, so a message can be sent to someone's phone through email.

questions: how to put a phone number in an email address
subtitle: How to write a phone number as an email address for gateways

tldr.problem: Email systems can reach people on the internet, but phone networks operate separately. Services need a standard way to send messages to phones through email gateways.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2303 defines a minimal format that encodes a PSTN phone number in the local part of an email address using a service identifier and phone number, plus optional extensions for extra fields.
tldr.outcome: Email gateways to phones can now work with a standard address format, allowing emails to reach phone users. RFC 3191 replaced this specification with improvements.

facts.label: Global phone format
facts.value: Plus sign followed by digits, hyphens, or dots

facts.label: Service selector
facts.value: Case-insensitive identifier like VOICE, FAX, or SMS

today: RFC 2303 was superseded by RFC 3191, which improved the minimal PSTN address format in Internet Mail. The newer specification is now the standard for encoding phone numbers as email addresses.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC describes a minimal standard format for encoding PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network) addresses into email addresses. The goal is to let email users send messages to phones through email gateways, and to enable email networks to be used as a transport for messages destined for phone numbers, reducing the cost of long-distance PSTN calls.

Unlike full PSTN-to-email conversion, which is more complex, this specification provides only the minimum required addressing method. It includes an extension mechanism so service-specific specifications can add additional fields as needed.
sections.eli5: The standard is a simple recipe for putting a phone number in an email address so gateways can send the email to the right phone service and phone number.

sections.title: PSTN Address Format
sections.content:
The minimal PSTN address has two parts: a service selector and a global phone number, separated by an equals sign. The service selector is a name like VOICE, FAX, or SMS (case-insensitive) that tells the gateway which service to use. The global phone number starts with a + and contains digits, with optional separators (hyphens or dots) for readability.

The format looks like VOICE=+1-202-765-3000. Each service type must have its own specification defining what service selector it uses and what optional fields it may include. The separators in the phone number are for user convenience; implementations must remove them before processing.
sections.eli5: The address has a service name and a phone number starting with a plus sign. It is like writing a label for the type of phone service and then the number to reach.

sections.title: Extensions and Options
sections.content:
Each PSTN address can include optional extensions in the form /keyword=value. These extensions let service-specific standards add extra information. For example, RFC 2303 mentions a FAX extension T33S=6377 that adds additional routing information for fax services, following ITU T.33 recommendations.

When implementations receive extensions they do not recognize, they must preserve them. Implementations that only support the minimal specification can ignore non-minimal extensions. This design lets the standard evolve without breaking existing systems.
sections.eli5: You can add extra instructions by using a slash and a keyword, like /T33S=6377 for fax machines that need a subaddress to route the call to the right place.

sections.title: Complete Email Address
sections.content:
The complete email address, called pstn-email, combines the PSTN address with an email domain. The format is VOICE=+1-202-765-3000@example.com. The part before the @ sign (the local part) contains the encoded phone number and follows the quoting rules of RFC 822 and RFC 1123. The part after the @ (the domain) must be a valid email domain that identifies the PSTN gateway service.

Optional slashes can appear at the start or end of the PSTN address for compatibility with other gateway standards, but implementations should not generate them. When multiple subaddresses are needed for one service, multiple email addresses must be used.
sections.eli5: The complete address looks like a normal email address, but instead of a person's name you put the phone number with a service type before the @ sign.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The main security concern is that email routing is determined by DNS lookups. An attacker who compromises a DNS server, forges a DNS response, or returns incorrect DNS information could force email messages destined for a phone gateway through an untrusted intermediary, where mail security could be compromised.

To mitigate this risk, clients should ensure mail routing is based only on authoritative DNS answers. As DNS Security mechanisms become more widely deployed, clients should use them to verify the authenticity and integrity of mail routing records.
sections.eli5: If someone tricks the email system about which server is the phone gateway, they could intercept the message. Use trusted DNS to find the real gateway.
